stem:
A 62-year-old woman wakes at 06:30 with slurred speech and weakness of her left arm. Her husband says she went to bed at 23:00 and seemed completely normal. The ambulance crew bring her to the emergency department, where the stroke team is activated and a CT head is arranged.

Which piece of history is the most important when deciding whether she can have acute reperfusion treatment?

options.A: When she was last known to be symptom free
options.B: Her family history of heart disease
options.C: How many years she has smoked cigarettes
options.D: Her typical sleep pattern over recent months
options.E: The age at which her menopause began

correct_answer: A. When she was last known to be symptom free
why_correct: Eligibility for thrombolysis and thrombectomy depends on how long ago the stroke started. When onset was not witnessed, as with a wake-up stroke, the clock starts from the time the person was last known to be well, and treatment decisions are then guided by that time and by imaging. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, 2022.
why_wrong: B. Family history helps with long-term prevention but does not decide acute eligibility. C. Smoking history is a risk factor and does not set the treatment window. D. Her sleep habits do not alter how reperfusion eligibility is judged. E. Menopausal history is irrelevant to the acute decision.
pearl: If onset is unwitnessed, including a wake-up stroke, use the last time the patient was known to be well, not the time they were found.
thinking: Symptoms found on waking  ↓  onset unwitnessed  ↓  work out when she was last known to be well  ↓  that time plus imaging guides thrombolysis and thrombectomy.
exam_trap: Using the time she woke up or arrived in hospital as onset underestimates the true interval and can lead to treatment outside its safe window.
takeaway: For unwitnessed onset, always document the last time the patient was known to be well, because it drives reperfusion decisions.
notes: Reangled to an unwitnessed wake-up stroke so the item cannot be answered by guesswork; no timing thresholds are asked. Verified NG128 wording ('last known to be well', wake-up strokes included). Key moved to A per plan. Live bank: NEU048 mentions 'last seen well' but tests thrombolysis; no item on last-known-well. Source key sound.
sources: carried over from source: NICE NG128

stem:
A 66-year-old woman was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease by a specialist three years ago and takes co-careldopa. She asks why she has had long-standing constipation, has lost her sense of smell and sometimes shouts out and moves her arms in her sleep. Her bowel habit has otherwise been stable and she has no weight loss or rectal bleeding.

How are these symptoms best described?

options.A: Unrelated age-related changes that are not part of her condition
options.B: Adverse effects of her levodopa that need the drug stopped at once
options.C: Features of a second neurodegenerative disorder developing alongside
options.D: Warning signs of a bowel tumour needing urgent cancer pathway referral
options.E: Recognised non-motor manifestations of Parkinson's disease itself

correct_answer: E. Recognised non-motor manifestations of Parkinson's disease itself
why_correct: Parkinson's disease is more than a movement disorder. Constipation, loss of smell (hyposmia), disturbed sleep including REM sleep behaviour disorder, low mood and autonomic problems are well-recognised non-motor features, and several can precede the tremor and slowness. Recognising them allows each to be asked about and treated. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, 2017 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. Attributing them to ageing misses treatable features of the disease. B. Levodopa can cause nausea and hypotension, but loss of smell and dream enactment are not drug effects, and stopping it abruptly is dangerous. C. Nothing suggests a second disorder, as these symptoms are part of the Parkinson's picture. D. A stable bowel habit without red-flag features does not suggest bowel cancer.
pearl: Hyposmia, constipation and REM sleep behaviour disorder can appear years before the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
thinking: Known Parkinson's disease  ↓  constipation, anosmia and dream enactment  ↓  none are motor signs  ↓  no red flags for bowel malignancy  ↓  non-motor features of the disease.
exam_trap: Choosing the cancer-pathway option because of constipation, when the habit is stable and there are no alarm features.
takeaway: Constipation, loss of smell and sleep disturbance are recognised non-motor features of Parkinson's disease, not separate problems.
notes: Rewritten as a vignette with REM sleep behaviour disorder added as a third non-motor feature and red-flag absence stated; key unchanged (non-motor manifestations). Source was a bare one-liner. No live PLAB 1 item tests non-motor features (PAN6451 is laxative mechanism, PAQ15228/PAQ941 volvulus). NICE NG71 page could not be fetched by curl in this session; content checked against recollection of NG71 and CKS, no change from source.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman wakes with weakness of the whole of the right side of her face, including her forehead. Bell's palsy is diagnosed and she starts oral prednisolone. Her right eye does not close fully when she blinks or sleeps, and it waters in the day. She is advised to use lubricating eye drops and to tape the eye closed at night.

What is the main eye complication this advice aims to prevent?

options.A: Raised intraocular pressure causing acute glaucoma
options.B: Retinal detachment from facial muscle traction
options.C: Optic nerve inflammation causing visual loss
options.D: Lens opacity developing from steroid treatment
options.E: Corneal drying and ulceration from lid exposure

correct_answer: E. Corneal drying and ulceration from lid exposure
why_correct: Facial nerve weakness stops the eyelid closing properly, so the cornea is exposed and dries, especially overnight. This risks keratopathy, ulceration and permanent visual damage, so eye protection with lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping at night is advised from the start, with prompt ophthalmology review if the eye becomes painful or red. Source: NICE CKS, Bell's palsy, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Angle-closure glaucoma is not caused by facial palsy. B. Retinal detachment is unrelated to the facial nerve or the eyelid muscles. C. Optic neuritis involves the optic nerve, not the facial nerve. D. Cataract from steroids needs prolonged high-dose use, not a short course, and is not the aim of eye protection.
pearl: The patient cannot protect the cornea if the blink and lid closure are lost, so protect it for them.
thinking: Facial nerve palsy  ↓  incomplete eyelid closure  ↓  cornea exposed and dry  ↓  lubricate by day, tape and ointment at night  ↓  prevent exposure keratopathy.
exam_trap: Choosing the steroid-related cataract because the patient is on prednisolone.
takeaway: In Bell's palsy the eye needs active protection because incomplete closure exposes the cornea to damage.
notes: Source was a bare one-liner; built a vignette so that the key is exposure of the cornea. Live NEU033/NEU063/PAAKT049 test eye protection as part of Bell's palsy management and DS134 tests the red painful eye, so topic overlap exists; the angle here is the complication that eye care prevents. PAN2278 (same learning point) is returned as skip to avoid repetition inside this file. CKS page not fetched by curl.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman reports that she copes well with stairs in the morning but struggles by the evening. Her arms tire when brushing her hair, and her voice becomes quieter and slurred if she reads aloud for a few minutes. Resting for a while helps. Tone, reflexes and sensation are normal, and her creatine kinase is normal.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Weakness that builds with repeated or sustained activity, including bulbar fatigue, and recovers with rest is the hallmark of myasthenia gravis, an antibody-mediated disorder of the neuromuscular junction. Reflexes and sensation are typically preserved and creatine kinase is normal. Diagnosis is supported by acetylcholine receptor antibodies, with further tests if these are negative. Source: NICE CKS, Myasthenia gravis, and Association of British Neurologists guidance.
why_wrong: A. Polymyositis causes painless proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase, without fatigability. B. Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness with reduced reflexes over days, not weakness that varies through the day. D. Motor neurone disease causes progressive weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs, not recovery with rest. E. Multiple sclerosis causes relapsing deficits separated in time and place, not weakness that recovers within minutes of rest.
pearl: Fatigability with recovery on rest points to the neuromuscular junction, not to muscle or nerve.
thinking: Weakness worse with use, better with rest  ↓  Bulbar and proximal involvement, normal reflexes and CK  ↓  Neuromuscular junction disorder  ↓  Myasthenia gravis
exam_trap: Choosing polymyositis because of proximal weakness, forgetting that fatigability and a normal creatine kinase point elsewhere.
takeaway: Fatigable proximal and bulbar weakness that improves with rest, with normal reflexes and sensation, is myasthenia gravis until proven otherwise.
notes: New vignette adds bulbar fatigue and normal CK/reflexes; non-ocular presentation chosen to avoid duplicating live ocular items (NEU022, BX070, PAQ16007). Source's 'peripheral arterial disease' and 'Parkinson's' distractors replaced with neuromuscular differentials. No figures. Citation is general (CKS geo-blocked); clinical content standard. Also stands in for PAN8595 (neuromuscular junction site).

stem:
A 79-year-old woman has had Parkinson's disease for eight years. She tells her GP that she occasionally sees a cat on the sofa that is not there. She knows it is not real, is not troubled by it, and her husband is relaxed about it. Her medicines have not changed for two years and she is otherwise well.

What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Start low-dose olanzapine to stop the symptoms progressing
options.B: Stop her co-careldopa until the hallucinations have settled
options.C: Start low-dose haloperidol each evening to suppress the symptoms
options.D: Start low-dose quetiapine and review in a month's time
options.E: Check for medical triggers; do not treat tolerated symptoms

correct_answer: E. Check for medical triggers; do not treat tolerated symptoms
why_correct: NICE advises a general medical evaluation for anyone with Parkinson's hallucinations and treatment of any trigger found, such as infection. If the hallucinations are well tolerated by the patient and family, they should not be treated. Treatment is considered only if they become distressing, and then involves specialist-guided dose reduction and quetiapine or clozapine. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, 2017 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. Olanzapine should not be offered for Parkinson's psychosis because it worsens motor function. B. Dopaminergic treatment must not be withdrawn abruptly because of the risk of acute akinesia or a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome. C. Haloperidol and other dopamine-blocking antipsychotics can severely worsen parkinsonism. D. Quetiapine is an option for distressing symptoms but is not needed when they are tolerated.
pearl: Tolerated hallucinations in Parkinson's disease do not need an antipsychotic; look for a trigger first.
thinking: Parkinson's disease with insightful visual hallucinations  ↓  Medical or drug trigger?  ↓  Tolerated by patient and family  ↓  Do not treat
exam_trap: Reaching for an antipsychotic or stopping dopaminergic drugs when the hallucinations are not distressing.
takeaway: Evaluate for triggers, and withhold treatment if hallucinations are well tolerated.
notes: NG71 recommendations 1.5.13-1.5.20 checked (general medical evaluation; do not treat if well tolerated; reduce triggering drugs with specialist advice; quetiapine/clozapine; do not offer olanzapine; other antipsychotics worsen motor features). Quetiapine made a distractor (reasonable only for distressing symptoms). Sibling items PAN1236 and PAN640 skipped as the same learning point. Distinct from PAQ15469/PAQ16456 (cause of hallucinations after ropinirole) and COE006 (Lewy body, avoid antipsychotics).

stem:
A 24-year-old woman has had several throbbing headaches over the past year, each starting on one side and lasting about half a day. During attacks she feels sick, cannot tolerate bright light and prefers to lie in a dark room. She has no visual symptoms beforehand, is entirely well between attacks, and her neurological examination is normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches lasting hours, with nausea and sensitivity to light, and complete recovery between attacks, fit migraine without aura. The normal examination and absence of red flags make a secondary cause unlikely. Source: NICE CKS, Migraine - diagnosis, 2024; NICE CG150, Headaches in over 12s, 2012.
why_wrong: A. Cluster headache causes short, very severe orbital pain with ipsilateral tearing and restlessness, mostly in men. B. Tension-type headache is bilateral, pressing and not accompanied by nausea or marked photophobia. C. Medication-overuse headache is a near-daily headache in someone taking acute analgesics frequently. D. Giant cell arteritis affects people over 50 and causes scalp tenderness and jaw claudication.
pearl: Migraine is a clinical diagnosis: a stereotyped attack with nausea and photophobia and a normal examination between attacks needs no imaging.
thinking: Recurrent stereotyped headaches  ↓  Unilateral, throbbing, nausea, photophobia  ↓  Normal between attacks, no red flags  ↓  Migraine without aura
exam_trap: Over-investigating a typical migraine, or missing that aura is not required for the diagnosis.
takeaway: Recurrent throbbing unilateral headache with nausea and photophobia and a normal examination is migraine; aura is not needed.
notes: Source and PAN766 are both migraine-diagnosis items; PAN766 skipped as a within-batch repeat. Vignette rebuilt (female, attack duration and normal examination added).

stem:
A 38-year-old man attends his GP surgery with four days of tingling in his feet followed by weakness of both legs. He now needs to hold the banister to climb stairs. He had a diarrhoeal illness two weeks ago. Examination shows symmetrical leg weakness and absent ankle reflexes, with normal speech and swallowing.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Request nerve conduction studies through the routine neurology outpatient service
options.B: Start oral prednisolone and review in the practice clinic after a week
options.C: Check vitamin B12, thyroid function and creatine kinase, then review in a fortnight
options.D: Refer immediately for hospital neurological assessment with respiratory monitoring
options.E: Refer to community physiotherapy and recheck muscle strength after a month

correct_answer: D. Refer immediately for hospital neurological assessment with respiratory monitoring
why_correct: Rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness over days with areflexia after an infection suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome, which can quickly cause respiratory and bulbar failure. NICE advises immediate referral for neurological assessment, where forced vital capacity and swallowing can be monitored. Source: NICE NG127, Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Routine outpatient nerve studies would leave a potentially life-threatening condition unmonitored. B. Corticosteroids do not help Guillain-Barre syndrome and the delay is unsafe. C. Waiting a fortnight for blood tests risks respiratory failure in the meantime. E. Physiotherapy and a month's delay is not appropriate for evolving paralysis.
pearl: Speed of progression decides the urgency: weakness developing over days warrants same-day hospital assessment even when the patient is currently walking.
thinking: Symmetrical weakness progressing over days  ↓  Areflexia, recent diarrhoea  ↓  Possible Guillain-Barre syndrome  ↓  Immediate hospital assessment
exam_trap: Being reassured because breathing and swallowing are currently normal, when deterioration can be rapid.
takeaway: Rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness needs immediate referral for neurological assessment, because respiratory failure can develop quickly.
notes: Source said 'over three weeks'; NG127 1.10.2 specifies progression within hours to days, so the timeline was changed to four days. Key is the referral-urgency principle, distinct from live BX426/NEU102/NEU021 (diagnosis, treatment, FVC monitoring). PAN1695 (GBS recognition) skipped as duplicate of BX426.

presentation: Loss of smell after head injury
stem:
A 31-year-old cyclist was knocked off his bike and struck the front of his helmet. He was admitted overnight with a mild head injury and CT of the brain was normal. Two weeks later he tells his GP that food tastes bland and he can no longer smell coffee, although his vision, hearing and facial movements are normal.

Which structure is most likely to have been injured?

options.A: The trigeminal nerve branches supplying the nasal mucosa
options.B: The vestibulocochlear nerve within the petrous temporal bone
options.C: The facial nerve within the facial canal of the temporal bone
options.D: The optic chiasm above the pituitary fossa
options.E: The olfactory nerve fibres crossing the cribriform plate

correct_answer: E. The olfactory nerve fibres crossing the cribriform plate
why_correct: Anosmia after head trauma is typically caused by shearing of the delicate olfactory nerve fibres as they pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, and it can occur even when CT is normal. Taste seems reduced because flavour depends heavily on smell, so a bland taste with normal facial and visual function points to olfactory nerve injury. Source: standard neuroanatomy; NICE NG232, Head injury, 2023 (assessment and complications).
why_wrong: A. Trigeminal branches carry nasal sensation (for example, to irritants), not the sense of smell. B. Vestibulocochlear injury causes hearing loss, tinnitus or vertigo, which he does not have. C. Facial nerve injury causes facial weakness and altered taste from the anterior tongue, but his face moves normally. D. Chiasmal injury would cause visual field loss, which is absent here.
pearl: Anosmia after a frontal blow or fall is a classic sign of cribriform plate injury and may be the only neurological finding.
thinking: Head injury  ↓  loss of smell and bland food  ↓  other cranial nerve functions normal  ↓  shearing of olfactory fibres at the cribriform plate.
exam_trap: Taste complaints can mislead candidates into choosing the facial nerve, but flavour loss usually reflects smell loss.
takeaway: Isolated loss of smell after head trauma points to the olfactory nerve at the cribriform plate.
notes: New vignette (cyclist, normal CT, two-week history) testing the same fact as the source. Source options had 'only' qualifiers that were removed; all options rewritten as site-specific structures of similar length. Anatomy is standard; NICE NG232 is the acute head injury guideline (no figures involved).

stem:
A 38-year-old teacher has had several months of involuntary contractions of her neck muscles that twist her head to the right and tilt it slightly upwards. The posture can be partially relieved by lightly touching her chin. She has no weakness, sensory loss or tremor at rest, and she has taken no antipsychotic or antiemetic drugs.

Which term best describes this movement disorder?
why_correct: Dystonia is a movement disorder in which sustained or intermittent muscle contractions cause twisting movements and abnormal postures, and focal neck involvement is called cervical dystonia. A sensory trick, such as touching the chin to ease the posture, is characteristic. Source: NHS, Dystonia; Association of British Neurologists teaching on movement disorders.
why_wrong: A. Tremor is a rhythmic oscillation of a body part rather than a sustained twisting posture. C. Chorea consists of irregular, brief, flowing and unpredictable movements that move from one body part to another. D. Myoclonus consists of sudden, brief, shock-like jerks, not sustained postures. E. Tics are repetitive, stereotyped movements or sounds that can be briefly suppressed and are preceded by an urge.
pearl: A sensory trick that eases the posture is a useful bedside clue to dystonia.
thinking: Sustained twisting neck posture  ↓  eased by touching the chin  ↓  not rhythmic, brief or jerky  ↓  dystonia (cervical).
exam_trap: Candidates may pick tremor because the head is moving, but the key feature is the sustained posture.
takeaway: Sustained or intermittent muscle contraction producing twisting movements and abnormal postures is dystonia.
notes: Source options mixed unrelated terms (aphasia, paraesthesia); replaced with movement-disorder terms so distractors are plausible. Added drug history to exclude acute drug-induced dystonia. Single-word options; key is mid-length. Live NEU079/P072 cover drug-induced acute dystonia (treatment), not recognition of dystonia as a term. No NICE guideline for dystonia recognition; NHS page cited.

presentation: Knee extension weakness and L3-L4 root
stem:
A 58-year-old man has had two weeks of pain across the front of his thigh and inner shin. On examination he cannot fully straighten his right knee against resistance, the right knee jerk is reduced, and the ankle jerk and ankle movements are normal. MRI is arranged to look for nerve root compression.

Which nerve root is most likely to be affected?

options.A: L5 root, as in a typical sciatic-type disc prolapse
options.B: L3 and L4 roots, supplying the quadriceps
options.C: S1 root, supplying the calf muscles
options.E: L1 root, supplying the hip flexor muscles

correct_answer: B. L3 and L4 roots, supplying the quadriceps
why_correct: Straightening the knee depends on the quadriceps, which is supplied by the femoral nerve from the L3 and L4 roots, and the knee jerk is mediated by the same roots. Weak knee extension with a reduced knee jerk and normal ankle findings therefore localises to L3-L4. Source: Standard myotome and reflex levels, Medical Research Council scale and UK undergraduate clinical neurology teaching.
why_wrong: A. L5 mainly controls ankle and big-toe dorsiflexion and hip abduction, and does not explain the weak knee extension or the reduced knee jerk. C. S1 supplies plantarflexion and the ankle jerk, which are normal here. D. The hamstrings bend the knee rather than straighten it, so S2 does not fit. E. L1 contributes to hip flexion and groin sensation, not to the quadriceps.
pearl: Knee jerk is L3-L4 and ankle jerk is S1-S2; matching the reflex to the weak movement fixes the level.
thinking: Weak knee extension  ↓  quadriceps / femoral nerve  ↓  knee jerk reduced  ↓  root level L3-L4
exam_trap: Choosing L5 because it is the commonest lumbar root in sciatica, when the weakness is at the knee and the ankle examination is normal.
takeaway: Knee extension and the knee jerk are L3-L4; ankle dorsiflexion is L4-L5 and the ankle jerk is S1.
notes: Source was a one-line recall item; rebuilt as a root-localisation vignette (root compression) rather than a nerve-name question, so it does not repeat BX643 (femoral nerve after pelvic surgery). Source key L3-L4 is correct. No guideline exists for myotome levels; citation is standard teaching.
sources: Standard myotome/reflex tables (MRC); clinical neurological examination teaching

stem:
A 35-year-old man with known epilepsy has a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure at home. When paramedics arrive, his left arm and leg are weak. His weakness gradually improves over several hours and has fully resolved by the next morning. A CT head scan is normal.

What is the most likely explanation for the weakness?

options.E: Acute demyelination of the right hemisphere

why_correct: Temporary focal weakness lasting minutes to hours after a seizure is Todd's paresis (postictal paralysis), thought to reflect neuronal exhaustion in the area that seized. It resolves spontaneously, and a normal scan with a clear temporal relationship to a witnessed seizure supports it. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. A transient ischaemic attack can cause temporary weakness, but here the weakness began straight after a convulsion and evolved gradually, which points to a postictal cause. B. Hemiplegic migraine follows a headache and aura rather than a generalised convulsion. C. Functional weakness is a diagnosis of exclusion and is not suggested by a witnessed seizure in a known epileptic. E. Demyelination evolves over days and does not resolve within hours.
pearl: Todd's paresis lasts from minutes to a day or so; persistent weakness should prompt imaging for stroke or other structural causes.
thinking: Known epilepsy and witnessed seizure  ↓  hemiparesis afterwards  ↓  improves over hours  ↓  Todd's paresis
exam_trap: Labelling post-seizure weakness as a stroke or TIA without recognising the postictal pattern.
takeaway: Transient focal weakness after a seizure that resolves over hours is Todd's paresis.
notes: Source distractors were unrelated diagnoses; replaced with plausible competing causes of transient hemiweakness. Plan puts the key at D. NG217 does not name Todd's paresis explicitly; citation is for the epilepsy context, the term is standard neurology teaching.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman who had an episode of optic neuritis last year describes brief electric-shock sensations that shoot down her back and into both legs whenever she bends her head forward to read her phone. The sensation stops as soon as she lifts her head. Neurological examination today is normal.

Which named clinical phenomenon does this describe?
why_correct: Lhermitte sign is a brief electric-shock sensation running down the spine and limbs on neck flexion. It reflects irritability of demyelinated dorsal column pathways in the cervical cord and is classically described in multiple sclerosis, which fits her earlier optic neuritis. It can also occur with other cervical cord disease. Source: NICE CKS, Multiple sclerosis (clinical features), reviewed 2024.
why_wrong: A. Uhthoff phenomenon is temporary worsening of existing symptoms when body temperature rises, for example with a hot bath or fever. B. Romberg sign is loss of balance with the eyes closed, indicating impaired joint position sense. C. Tinel sign is tingling produced by tapping over an entrapped peripheral nerve, such as the median nerve at the wrist. E. Babinski response is an upgoing great toe on plantar stimulation and signals an upper motor neurone lesion.
pearl: Neck-flexion electric shocks in a young adult with previous optic neuritis should prompt thought of demyelination in the cervical cord.
thinking: Brief electric shock on neck flexion  ↓  cervical cord dorsal column irritability  ↓  Lhermitte sign  ↓  think multiple sclerosis (other cord disease possible).
exam_trap: Uhthoff phenomenon is also an MS eponym, but it is triggered by heat rather than by neck flexion.
takeaway: Electric-shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion is Lhermitte sign, a feature of cervical cord pathology such as multiple sclerosis.
notes: Re-angled from a bare eponym recall to a short clinical vignette with an MS clue; distractors changed (Uhthoff added, Murphy dropped). Clinical content carried over unchanged. No live PLAB 1 question tests Lhermitte sign (grep). Eponym itself not guideline-dependent; CKS cited generally, not re-fetched.

stem:
A 75-year-old right-handed woman is brought in after her husband found that she could not follow any of his instructions. She talks freely in long, well-formed sentences that include invented words and make little sense. Her limb strength is normal. Imaging confirms a recent infarct.

In which area of the brain is the infarct most likely to lie?
why_correct: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension is receptive (Wernicke) aphasia. Wernicke area lies in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the language-dominant hemisphere, which is the left in almost all right-handed people. Because the motor cortex is spared, limb strength is often normal. Source: Royal College of Physicians, National Clinical Guideline for Stroke, 2023 (communication disorders); standard neuroanatomy.
why_wrong: A. The left inferior frontal gyrus is Broca area, whose damage gives effortful non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension. B. The right parietal lobe is associated with neglect and visuospatial problems rather than language loss. C. The left occipital lobe supplies the right visual field and does not produce fluent nonsensical speech. D. The cerebellar vermis affects truncal balance and gait, not language.
pearl: Fluent nonsense plus poor comprehension points to the dominant temporal lobe, whereas non-fluent speech points to the frontal lobe.
thinking: Fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension  ↓  Wernicke aphasia  ↓  dominant (left) posterior superior temporal gyrus.
exam_trap: Choosing the frontal lobe because speech is the main complaint ignores that fluency and comprehension separate temporal from frontal lesions.
takeaway: Wernicke aphasia localises to the language-dominant posterior temporal region; Broca aphasia localises to the inferior frontal gyrus.
notes: Learning point is lesion localisation of Wernicke aphasia (live BX169 asks for the aphasia type, not the location; PAQ15259 covers Broca location only). Source distractors reworded; right-handed specified so dominant side is unambiguous. Established neuroanatomy, not re-fetched.

stem:
A 66-year-old man with hypertension and a long smoking history has had three brief episodes this week, each lasting under ten minutes, of double vision, slurred speech and feeling unsteady on his feet. He is completely well between episodes and neurological examination today is normal.

Which arterial territory is most likely to be involved?

options.C: Ophthalmic branch of the internal carotid artery
options.D: Anterior spinal artery supplying the cord

correct_answer: E. Vertebrobasilar system supplying the brainstem
why_correct: Diplopia, dysarthria and imbalance arise from brainstem and cerebellar dysfunction, supplied by the vertebrobasilar (posterior) circulation. Fully resolving episodes in a patient with vascular risk factors indicate transient ischaemic attacks in this territory, which carry a high early stroke risk and need urgent specialist assessment. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Anterior cerebral artery ischaemia mainly causes leg weakness and behavioural change. B. Middle cerebral artery ischaemia typically causes contralateral face and arm weakness, sensory loss and dysphasia or neglect. C. Ophthalmic branch involvement causes transient monocular visual loss, not binocular diplopia. D. Anterior spinal artery ischaemia affects the cord and spares speech and eye movements.
pearl: Double vision with slurred speech and imbalance localises to the brainstem and posterior circulation.
thinking: Diplopia plus dysarthria plus ataxia  ↓  brainstem and cerebellum  ↓  vertebrobasilar territory  ↓  transient episodes mean posterior circulation TIA needing urgent assessment.
exam_trap: Choosing the middle cerebral artery because it is the commonest stroke territory, although the symptoms are brainstem features.
takeaway: Brainstem symptoms such as diplopia, dysarthria and ataxia point to the vertebrobasilar circulation, even when they resolve.
notes: Key verified (standard neuroanatomy; NG128 on TIA). Re-angled from a bare recall item to a vignette of recurrent vertebrobasilar TIAs. Distinct from live BX919 (acute posterior circulation stroke with vertigo); mild overlap risk accepted.
